subtitulo: Distancing a claim without hiding behind it
descripcion: Beyond the basic passive, C1 English uses the impersonal it is + reporting verb pattern to attribute a claim without naming a source: it is said, it is believed, it is widely assumed. This is the register of journalism, policy writing and careful academic prose, and it fails when the pattern is used on facts that don't need distancing.

filas: It is believed that the figures are outdated.
The policy is thought to have failed.
signals a common but unverified view

ejemplos.texto: It is widely assumed that the figures will be revised downward.
The policy is thought to have failed for reasons unrelated to its design.
It is understood that no final decision has been made.

notas: The subject-first version (the policy is thought to have failed) reads slightly more formal and academic than the it-first version.
Widely, generally and commonly before the reporting verb signal that the view is common, not necessarily correct.
This pattern is for genuinely unattributed or collective views — using it on a claim you could simply state as fact reads as evasive.

es.en: Spanish achieves the same effect with «se cree que» or «se dice que», a single impersonal structure instead of two parallel forms (it is + verb, subject + is thought to). Spanish speakers usually learn only the it is pattern and miss the subject-initial variant, which is the more frequent one in English news and reports.
es.es: El español logra el mismo efecto con «se cree que» o «se dice que», una única estructura impersonal en vez de dos formas paralelas («it is + verb», «subject + is thought to»). Los hispanohablantes suelen aprender solo el patrón con «it is» y se pierden la variante con sujeto inicial, más frecuente en noticias e informes ingleses.

de.en: German has a perfect bridge for the subject-initial pattern: «sollen» in its reported sense («Er soll sehr reich sein» – He is said to be very rich). German speakers who map «soll» onto is said to / is thought to use the pattern naturally; the risk is translating «man sagt» as one says, which sounds stilted in English.
de.de: Für das Subjektmuster gibt es im Deutschen eine perfekte Brücke: «sollen» in berichtender Bedeutung («Er soll sehr reich sein» – «He is said to be very rich»). Wer «soll» mit «is said to / is thought to» verbindet, verwendet das Muster meist natürlich. Die Gefahr liegt darin, «man sagt» als «one says» zu übersetzen, was im Englischen steif klingt.

it.en: Italian uses «si dice che» and marks unconfirmed information with the «condizionale» («sarebbe molto ricco»). The typical calque is it is said that he would be very rich; the English subject-initial pattern (he is said to be…) has no direct Italian model and needs practice.
it.it: L'italiano usa «si dice che» e marca le informazioni non confermate con il condizionale («sarebbe molto ricco»). Il calco tipico è «it is said that he would be very rich»; il modello inglese con soggetto iniziale («he is said to be…») non ha un equivalente diretto e va praticato.

fr.en: French uses «on dit que», «il paraît que» and the «conditionnel» («il serait très riche»). «Il est censé être» corresponds well to he is supposed to be, but the neutral he is said to be has no direct French model, and «on dit» is often calqued as one says.
fr.fr: Le français utilise «on dit que», «il paraît que» et le conditionnel («il serait très riche»). «Il est censé être» correspond bien à «he is supposed to be», mais le neutre «he is said to be» n'a pas de modèle direct, et «on dit» est souvent calqué en «one says».

pt.en: Portuguese uses «diz-se que» or «dizem que», and «consta que» for unconfirmed information. The subject-initial pattern (he is said to be…) has no direct model and needs practice, as Portuguese speakers tend to stay with it is said that.
pt.pt: O português usa «diz-se que» ou «dizem que», e «consta que» para informação não confirmada. O padrão com sujeito inicial («he is said to be…») não tem um modelo direto e precisa ser praticado, pois falantes de português tendem a ficar com «it is said that».

errores: Using this pattern on a fact that doesn't need distancing, which reads as evasive.
Only using the it is + that version and never the subject-first is thought to version.
Dropping the infinitive after the subject-first pattern: the policy is thought failed instead of is thought to have failed.

es: «*se dice que*» rendered as *It says that* instead of *It is said that*.
de: Hearsay «*soll*» rendered as *shall*: *He shall have resigned* instead of *He is said to have resigned*.
«*man sagt*» rendered as *One says that* instead of *It is said that*.
it: «*si dice che*» rendered as *It says that* instead of *It is said that*.
fr: «*on dit que*» rendered as *One says that* instead of *It is said that*.
pt: «*diz-se que*» rendered as *It says that* instead of *It is said that*.

redemittel.funcion: flags a common but unverified view

traducciones.pt: Parte-se geralmente do princípio de que…

redemittel.expresion: It remains to be seen whether…

redemittel.funcion: questions what the impersonal form hides

mision.consigna: Write a short news analysis of a story that spread fast before anyone checked it — invented or generic, no real names or dates.
requisitos: three different impersonal reporting patterns (*it is believed that*, *is said to*, *it remains to be seen whether*)
one sentence where you deliberately do NOT distance, because the fact is verified — and say why
one sentence explaining how *fake news* differs from an honest error

microtareas.texto: Take three headlines from today and rewrite each with *it is claimed that* or *is reported to*. Which one got weaker, which got more honest?
Write five sentences with *is thought to have* + past participle about events whose *source* you haven't verified.
Record 90 seconds: how *public opinion* forms before the facts are in. Use at least two impersonal passives.

autochequeo: Is this pattern reserved for claims that genuinely need distancing?
Have I used both the it is + that and the subject-first is thought to forms?
Is the infinitive present after every subject-first pattern?
Would a reader sense evasion where a plain statement would have been more honest?
Is widely/generally/commonly used correctly to signal a common rather than a verified view?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on impersonal reporting patterns. Check whether they're used on claims that genuinely need distancing, and check the infinitive form after subject-first patterns. Do not rewrite the text.
